chapter_theme: Baseness (கீழ்மை): the base keep their nature whatever is done for them. Teaching, invitation, honour, wealth and care do not change them, and the chapter sets them beside the worthy, whom prosperity does not change either.
structure_note: Similes from animals and objects carry the argument: the hen (341), the dog (345), the jewelled sandal (347), the young bullocks (350). 343, 344, 346 and 349 set the worthy and the base side by side. 347 and 350 close on the same two lines.

341.reading: As a hen keeps scratching the rubbish heap though grain is poured into its mouth each morning, so the base man, however you lay open books full of weighty meaning for him, goes further along the way his mind likes.
341.nuance: மிகும் suggests excess, not just persistence: Mudaliar glosses it as going beyond bounds.

342.reading: Say to the base man 'let us go without delay to the faultless who hold firm learning', and he gets up and leaves saying 'let's sleep', or else refuses with some other excuse.
342.nuance: The comedy is in the excuses: sleep first, and failing that, anything else.

343.reading: Even if they gain great prosperity, the worthy keep one even course without falling from their nature; when the base gain it, the verse says only that they are 'able in one course', lord of the good land of shining waterfalls.
343.nuance: Pope agrees with Shanmuganar that the base man's conduct does not change. Mudaliar takes பெருநடை as wealth and records that others read it as great distinction.

positions.position: With prosperity the base man becomes adept at a conduct different from his earlier one.
With prosperity the base man keeps to his own low course.

344.reading: If they have enjoyed a good done to them, though it is only the size of a millet grain, the worthy think of it as a palm tree; but goods the size of a palm, done again and again, are no good at all to those who do not know a good, lord of the land of bright waterfalls.
344.nuance: Mudaliar cites Kural 104 and Parimelazhagar's remark that millet and palm are conventional measures of small and great.

345.reading: A dog, though reared on food from a golden bowl, watches unblinking for others' leftovers; so even if you treat the base as great, the deeds they do will be different.
345.nuance: The golden bowl is the honour shown: it changes the setting, not the appetite.

346.reading: Even with an emperor's wealth the excellent never speak a boastful word, but if a base man gains a காணி on top of a முந்திரி, he thinks himself Indra.
346.nuance: The two words are tiny fractions. Shanmuganar gives முந்திரி as 1/320 and காணி as 1/80; Mudaliar gives காணி as 1/64 and முந்திரி as a quarter of that, and allows the words to be read in the other order.

347.reading: Though a sandal is made of flawless gold set with fine gems, it is still for the foot; so the base, though they have come into wealth, are known by the deeds they do.
347.nuance: The sandal's material is the wealth and its place is the nature: costly making does not move it from the foot.

348.reading: The base are quick to speak harshly, have no kindly regard, rejoice in others' troubles, fly into rage again and again, go where they please and scorn everyone, lord of the good land of mighty hills.
348.nuance: A plain list with no image, which Mudaliar classes as straightforward description (தன்மை நவிற்சி).

349.reading: If people stand by them for many days, the worthy grow kind to them, thinking 'these are old friends'; the base feel no warmth and simply scorn them, lord of the cool shore of the roaring sea where the neydal breathes honey.
349.nuance: Mudaliar takes standing by someone as being subordinate and obedient to them, so the test is how each kind treats long-serving dependants.

350.reading: Hear, sir: small bullocks will never learn to wear the yoke and draw the cart however long you feed them cut grass, and the base, though they have come into wealth, are known by the deeds they do.
350.nuance: Care cannot supply a capacity that is not there; the bullocks are well fed and still small.

links.note: Both say study does not override what a person already is. In Parimelazhagar's reading 373 credits the lasting understanding to fate; 341 credits it to base nature.
Both use a domestic animal that keeps its habit despite good feeding: the hen to its rubbish heap, the dog to others' leftovers.
976 says the small have no thought of cherishing the great and taking them as guides; 342 shows the base man inventing excuses not to go to them.
On Shanmuganar's reading 343 matches 973: being placed high does not make the base high, nor does it change the worthy.
On Mudaliar's reading, prosperity turns the base man to a new course, as 977 says distinction falling to the unworthy turns into excess.
The first half restates 104 with the same millet and palm, and Mudaliar cites it here.
105 says a benefit's measure is the worth of the one who receives it; 344's second half shows that measure at zero, with palm-sized help counting for nothing among the ungrateful.
978 says greatness always bows and smallness admires itself; 346 shows both, with an emperor's wealth on one side and a fraction of a coin on the other.
963 asks for humility in abundance; 346's worthy keep it even with an emperor's wealth.
505 makes one's deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness; 347 and 350 apply it to the base who have grown rich, whose wealth cannot hide what their deeds show.
1079's base man finds fault on seeing others well fed and clothed; 348's rejoices when others suffer. They are the same envy seen from both sides.
810 praises those who do not change toward old friends; 349 gives the worthy that constancy and shows the base without it.
The two share their closing lines word for word: 347 makes the point with an object, the jewelled sandal, and 350 with an animal, the young bullocks.

source_issues: Quatrains 347 and 350 end with the same two lines (எய்திய செல்வத்த ராயினும் கீழ்களைச் செய்தொழிலாற் காணப் படும்). Mudaliar glosses them only under 347; Shanmuganar and Pope translate them under both. This may be the tradition's own repetition or a copying error.
Quatrain 345: Mudaliar's gloss reads யாதுகாத்துவரினும், apparently for பாதுகாத்துவரினும்.
Quatrain 348: Pope's translation is not aligned.
